$$

$$

$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Computing Two Iterations of the Newton-Raphson Method
canonical_examples.problem:
Suppose we wish to find a zero of the function $\boldsymbol{f}(x,y)$ in the region $[1,3] \times [-2,0] \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,$ where
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14074434/assets/891b79a977ea7d9f4062d3614d7001ade71cfc10de54fcbae6608eebed7e8d1a.png)
Calculate the second iteration of the Newton-Raphson process that starts at $\mathbf x_0 = \big[1, \: 0 \big]^T$ if the first iteration of the algorithm gives $\mathbf{x}_1 = \big[ 3, \: -1 \big]^T.$ Round your final answer to three decimal places (if needed).
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $\boldsymbol{f} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [J_\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n),
$$

where $J_\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)$ is the Jacobian of $\boldsymbol f$ evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_n.$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+y-4) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+y-4) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(x+{y}^{2}-3) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(x+{y}^{2}-3)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2x & 1 \\ 1 & 2y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14074434/assets/95e234c5c9b32e1ea965f1cd184563699fbd2793d51a9d1e4ec96ffb4e42dc50.png)

For the second iteration, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-{[\begin{aligned}2x & 1 \\ 1 & 2y\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{1}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+y-4 \\ x+{y}^{2}-3\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{1}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}2(3) & 1 \\ 1 & 2(-1)\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}{3}^{2}+(-1)-4 \\ 3+(-1)^{2}-3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{6\cdot (-2)-1\cdot 1}[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ -1 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{13}[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{30}{13} \\ -\frac{11}{13}\end{aligned}] \\  & ≈[\begin{aligned}2.308 \\ -0.846\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

Find the matrix equation that defines the first iteration of the Newton-Raphson process starting at the point $\big[ 1, \: 1 \big]^T,$ and compute the components of the first iteration.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $\boldsymbol{f} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [J_\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n),
$$

where $J_\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)$ is the Jacobian of $\boldsymbol f$ evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_n.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be re-written as 

$$
J_\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}-\mathbf{x}_n) = -\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n).
$$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy-1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2x & -2y \\ 2y & 2x\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14074434/assets/13f9eb9850462317be5a5c7da22fe53ee89b24d9ce1a9226c2d0ee1e6355ba19.png)

$$
\begin{aligned}{[\begin{aligned}2x & -2y \\ 2y & 2x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-{[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2} \\ 2xy-1\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}} \\ [\begin{aligned}2(1) & -2(1) \\ 2(1) & 2(1)\end{aligned}]({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-[\begin{aligned}(1)^{2}-(1)^{2} \\ 2(1)(1)-1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system of equations, we get ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14074434/assets/d5eb5a91fdd96bf6ca50539d2119a97ce9e5600b3114f708cda4d95a047e8b81.png) Hence,
